job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Jamal Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Jamal, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I wake up around nine in a rented room I split with two guys, Tomas and Reggie, in a three-bedroom near the university in Albuquerque. I do a couple of coding challenges, tweak my résumé for whatever posting I'm on, and apply to five or six jobs before noon. My software degree is done, I finished top of my year, but nobody has called back in four months. Afternoons I do shifts at a bike shop and the money covers my share of rent and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, that's a relief, but it doesn't fix hiring. Half the problem is the résumé filters that reject people before a human reads anything. I'd say that online and at the meetups, since a lot of us are fighting the same filter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a plateau means the market stays what it is now, and that's bad. I've got thirty-eight thousand dollars of loans, one internship at a state agency and one at a logistics startup, and still no offer. If AI is just hype, the tech companies keep cutting juniors anyway, because the money got expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, but smarter: fewer applications, each one with a note to a real person. I'd go to the Thursday developers' meetup and ask the guy from the state agency who liked my internship project. I use AI to tidy my cover letters now and then, which saves an hour. And I'd keep the bike shop shifts going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stuck, mostly. A bit embarrassed, honestly, when my aunt asks at dinner how the job's going. I know it's not my fault, but it feels like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You blamed the filters. Who built them, and what would you change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hiring-platform companies, and the firms that buy them to save recruiters' time. I'd want a rule that a human must look at every applicant who meets the listed requirements. It sounds boring but it would get me an interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your aunt next time she asks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth: I've sent two hundred applications, had four interviews and no offer, and I'm still trying. She worries a lot, so I'd skip the loan number.

say: Plateau is a relief, but it doesn't fix **hiring filters** that reject people unseen.
I'd say it at **meetups**, where plenty of people fight the same filter.
think: A plateau means the **market stays tight** while I carry thirty-eight thousand in loans.
Companies keep **cutting juniors** because money got expensive, hype or not.
do: Send **fewer, better applications** with a note to a real person.
Ask my **state agency contact** about openings at the Thursday meetup.
Keep the **bike shop shifts** and use AI only to tidy cover letters.
feel: **Stuck** and a bit embarrassed, even though it's not his fault.
S0.quote: I've sent two hundred applications, had four interviews and no offer, and I'm still trying.
fieldNote: Blames **hiring-filter software** and the firms that buy it.
Hides the **loan figure** from his aunt, like others in the cohort.

steps.text: Send fewer applications, each with a note to a real person
Use AI to tidy cover letters before sending them
Keep working shifts at the bike shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's already happening in tech and nobody wants to admit it. Fewer junior postings, more 'senior only' ads, and teams doing the same work with half the people. I'd say that workers need a seat at the table, not a pep talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think entry-level coding is exactly what it takes first. Writing small features, fixing bugs, writing tests: that was my internship at the logistics startup, and they told me the AI now does that. So my first job gets harder to find, even with top marks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work more with the tools, not less. Right now I use them now and then, so I'd get properly good at them, and build one real project for a nonprofit, like a scheduling tool for the food bank where I volunteer. I'd also join the tech workers' union chapter that's starting in town. And I'd look at jobs outside pure software, like data work in the health system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with some curiosity. If I can get through the door, the tools make me faster. The door is the issue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which job outside pure software would you take, and why that one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A data analyst post in the state health department. The pay is lower but it's stable, and it still needs someone who can code. They'd also train me on the job, which small startups don't do any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your two flatmates say about your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas would say take anything, he's been a barista for a year. Reggie would say go to another city. I'd say I can't afford a move without a job, so I'm going to build something that proves I can do the work.

say: Teams do the same work with **half the people**, and workers need a seat at the table.
Companies call it **efficiency** while junior postings disappear.
think: Entry-level work like **small features and tests** is what goes first.
My top marks may not be enough to get **through the door**.
do: Get **properly good** at AI tools instead of using them occasionally.
Build a **food bank scheduling tool** as a portfolio project.
Join the tech workers' **union chapter** and apply for state health data jobs.
feel: **Anxious but curious**, since tools help once he is inside.
S1.quote: If I can get through the door, the tools make me faster. The door is the issue.
fieldNote: Moves from **using** AI to mastering it, which fits his steady nature.
His **internship** at the startup gives him first-hand evidence.
Balances **union action** with a practical public-sector fallback.

steps.text: Practise with AI coding tools daily and build a portfolio project
Make a free scheduling tool for the food bank
Join the new tech workers' union chapter in town
Apply for data analyst posts in the state health department

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready and neither are the people in charge. Demand a public plan: income support, retraining paid for by the companies, and a rule that firms announce layoffs early. I'd say this online and sign every petition I could find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my whole degree becomes a very expensive piece of paper in about two years. The thinking work goes first, and coding is thinking work. A hands-on field might take longer, but I didn't study that, and I owe thirty-eight thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to land any job that gets me paid before 2028, even support work at the university IT desk. Then I'd move into something hands-on and physical: maybe robotics maintenance, since robots come three years later and somebody must service them. I'd ask my aunt about the spare room, which I hate doing. And I'd push my loan servicer for income-based repayment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Not dramatic scared, more like I keep checking my phone for news. I don't sleep well when I think about two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask your aunt for the spare room. What stops you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pride, mostly. Also she's forty minutes from the bike shop and I don't have a car. But if the choice is rent or the loan, I'd rather be in her spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years leave you that a longer warning wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means no second degree and no slow pivot. I pick whatever pays soonest and learn on the job. With longer I could take a retraining course without panic.

say: We aren't ready, and the people in charge are not ready either.
I'd back a **public plan** with income support and early layoff notice.
think: My degree becomes a **expensive piece of paper** within about two years.
Coding is **thinking work**, so it goes first, and the loan stays.
do: Take **any paid job** before 2028, even the university IT desk.
Move toward **robot maintenance**, since someone must service the machines.
Ask my aunt for her **spare room** and push for income-based repayment.
feel: **Scared**, constantly checking the news and sleeping badly.
S2.quote: I think my whole degree becomes a very expensive piece of paper in about two years.
fieldNote: Anxiety shows up as **news-checking**, not drama.
Considers **robot maintenance** as a way to ride the three-year gap.
Pride about the **spare room** is the real emotional cost.

steps.text: Apply for paid support jobs at the university IT desk
Study robot maintenance to service the machines arriving later
Ask my aunt about renting her spare room
Sign petitions and write to my senator about a public plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious, and five years is exactly enough to make a real plan if people push for one. Retraining funds, strong worker protections, maybe a shorter work week. I'd back any group that's organising on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd get a job, probably in the next year, and then I have maybe three years before it becomes shaky again. That's enough to pay down some of the loan and build skills that last, like systems work and being around hardware.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first sensible job, even if it isn't coding. Then I'd study evenings for a hardware-adjacent skill, like embedded systems or control, so I can move to the physical side. I'd put aside two hundred dollars a month for a cushion. And I'd help organise the union chapter so it has something to offer when people start losing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a little determined. It feels like a hard exam with a date, which I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why embedded systems and not something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it touches real machines and the robots arrive later. Software alone is the part AI gets good at first. Learning to wire a sensor and write code for it keeps me in the physical world a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would organising the chapter involve week to week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, boring stuff: a shared spreadsheet of job openings, a salary survey, a monthly meeting at a coffee place. But it gives people somewhere to go when they get laid off, which beats sitting alone.

say: Five years is **enough to plan** if people push for retraining and worker protections.
I'd back any group **organising** on this, including a shorter work week.
think: I'd likely find a job within the year, then have **about three years** before it gets shaky.
That window lets me **pay down loans** and build lasting skills.
do: Take the **first sensible job**, even if it isn't coding.
Study evenings in **embedded systems** to move toward hardware.
Set aside **two hundred dollars** monthly and help the union chapter.
feel: **Uneasy but determined**, like a hard exam with a date.
S3.quote: Learning to wire a sensor and write code for it keeps me in the physical world a bit longer.
fieldNote: Turns the **robot delay** into a career plan.
Wants the **union chapter** to offer practical support, such as job lists and salary surveys.
Mood stays **anxious** because he has no offer yet.

steps.text: Accept the first sensible job even outside coding
Study embedded systems in the evenings
Put aside two hundred dollars every month
Run the chapter's shared spreadsheet of job openings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, a decade is a real chance, but only if the rules get written early. Otherwise it's the same story as always: the companies get the gains and people get a lecture on resilience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be okay. I'd get a job, start paying the loans, maybe get a second degree or a licence. Ten years is longer than I've been planning anything, so it feels almost generous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a software job when one comes and learn it well, then use the first three years to build savings and a skill base. I'd look at moving to a city with more openings once I have a contract. I'd also volunteer on tech policy with the union and the food bank, since I'd like to do work that helps people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A little guilty, because friends from the bike shop don't have degrees and could be hit harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned friends from the bike shop. What would you want for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want training paid for and not a cheap course that leads nowhere. Two of my friends from the bike shop have mechanical skills that will last longer than my coding ever will, which is a funny thing to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with the two-year one, what's different in your first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd actually look for a good fit rather than a quick paycheck. I'd negotiate the first offer instead of accepting it in a panic. And I'd sleep.

say: A decade is a **real chance**, if the rules are written early.
Otherwise **companies take the gains** and people get lectured about resilience.
think: I'd probably be **okay**: a job, steady loan payments and maybe a licence.
Ten years is **longer** than I've ever planned, so it feels generous.
do: Take a software job and **build savings** during the first three years.
Move to a city with **more openings** once I have a contract.
Volunteer on **tech policy** with the union and food bank.
feel: **Mostly okay**, with some guilt for friends without degrees.
S4.quote: Two of my friends from the bike shop have mechanical skills that will last longer than my coding ever will
fieldNote: Mood eases because the **decade** gives room to bargain, not just survive.
Mentions **sleeping** again, which marks the calmer end of his range.

steps.text: Take a software job and learn it properly
Save half of each paycheck for the first three years
Move to a bigger city once I hold a contract
Volunteer on tech policy with the union and the food bank

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it leaves no room to choose. What would help is a public jobs guarantee for graduates, early notice from companies, and debt relief that doesn't wait for a crisis. Also a real person reading applications.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people my age don't want handouts. We want a fair shot at an entry job, and right now the system is deciding for us before we've had it.

headlineQuote: People my age don't want handouts. We want a fair shot at an entry job
portrait: Jamal is a **top software graduate** in Albuquerque with no offer after four months.
He shares a rented room with two flatmates and owes **thirty-eight thousand dollars**.
He works shifts at a **bike shop**, uses AI tools now and then, and has two internships behind him.
He blames **hiring filters** and companies that cut juniors, and wants unions and public plans.
He tries practical routes in each world: portfolio projects, **embedded skills**, state jobs and his aunt's spare room.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there is **no room to choose**.
whatWouldHelp: A **public jobs guarantee** and early layoff notice from companies.
A **human reader** for applications and debt relief before a crisis.
